description:
Hey guys! We are interested in space exploration, Earth systems, planets, and using creativity and technology to solve real-world challenges. Our goal is to develop an innovative idea for the challenge by exploring data, identifying patterns, and presenting our findings in an understandable way. 

We welcome team members who are interested. You don’t need to be an expert — curiosity, motivation, and teamwork are what matter most!

Let’s work together, share ideas, and build something amazing.
summary:
EarthTrend Explorer is a web app with a 3-D globe built on NASA data. Users pick any country or study area, and the app tests every variable for a trend: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant, with its uncertainty. It removes the seasonal cycle, requires two trend tests to agree, and corrects for testing many variables at once, so it does not mistake normal variability for a trend.

We used it for a study of soil moisture with NASA GLDAS data from Giovanni (2000-2026). On Hungary's Great Plain, root-zone soil moisture fell by 21 % although rainfall did not change, while the air warmed by 2.5 °C. In north-west China the same variable rose by 13 % under similar warming. This is a mirror trend, exactly as described in the challenge, and the difference between the two regions is significant (p = 0.001). The tool turns NASA data into a repeatable study for any place on Earth.
details:
What it does. The globe shows NASA Blue Marble imagery with country borders. Users search or click a country, or click a study-area marker. The side panel lists every variable with its trend per decade, the change in %, and a verdict: significant trend, possible trend, or no significant trend. A detail view shows the time series without its seasonal cycle, the trend line, Sen's slope with its 95 % range (the trend with its uncertainty), the total change and the p-values. Further tabs find which variables move together (Kendall tau, with and without long-term trends, corrected for autocorrelation and for testing many pairs) and run multiple regressions. "Compare regions" tests whether two regions trend in opposite directions and flags a mirror trend. Markers on the globe show the soil-moisture trend of each study area, and an arc links the mirror trend.

How significance works. The seasonal cycle is removed first. Two trend tests must agree: the Seasonal Kendall test and a Mann-Kendall test on yearly anomalies with the Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation. A false-discovery-rate correction is applied when many variables are tested. We checked the rule on simulated data without a trend: it says "significant" in about 5 % of cases, as a 5 % test should, while a plain regression line says so in 17-30 % of cases.

Our study. NASA GLDAS Noah v2.1 monthly data from Giovanni, January 2000 - July 2026, five regions on three continents.

  • Hungary (Homokhatsag, "Hungary's hidden desert"): root-zone soil moisture -21 % (significant), rainfall -8.5 % (no significant trend), air temperature +2.5 °C (significant). In summer about 38 litres less water under every square metre of soil than in the early 2000s. After accounting for rain and temperature, a drying trend remains.
  • North-west China (Tianshan foothills): root-zone soil moisture +13 % (significant) under similar warming and without a rainfall trend. The difference between Hungary and China is significant (p = 0.001).
  • Southern Sweden -12 % and northern Scotland -4 % (both significant, with less rain); Sahel: no significant trend.
  • In all five regions soil moisture rises with rain; in four it falls with heat. Same process, different long-term direction.
  • Robustness: Hungary stays at -20 to -23 % without the 2022 drought or when starting in 2003. The cause of China's wetting is still open: we tested a snowmelt explanation and the data did not support it. GLDAS is a land model; a next step is to check it against SMAP and GRACE satellite data.

Benefits and impact. The drying in Hungary is not caused by less rain, so waiting for wetter years will not solve it; water management is the lever. More generally, warming does not dry every soil the same way, so each region has to be tested. EarthTrend Explorer lets students, journalists and water or farming agencies do that in a few clicks, with honest statistics and plain-language results.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall), JavaScript (globe.gl, D3, Plotly), hosted on Render; code on GitHub.
